title: Letter Case Permutation
description: Generate every case permutation of a string's letters, using backtracking over a shared mutable character buffer.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given a string s, return all strings obtained by independently transforming every letter to either lowercase or uppercase; digits are left unchanged. Since multiple valid orderings exist, this document uses one specific deterministic backtracking order and shows its exact output.

blocks.caption: Each letter branches into two choices; each digit has only one, forming a decision tree whose leaves are the full output set.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","s (letters and digits)"],["Output","Every possible case-permutation string, any order accepted by the original problem"],["Digits","Unaffected, always pass through unchanged"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Generating every combination of independent binary choices (here, each letter's case) is the classic backtracking template: at each position, branch into every available choice, recurse, and undo the choice before trying the next one. A position with only one choice (a digit) simply has no branching at all.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This is one of the simplest forms of the backtracking template, useful as a foundation before tackling problems with pruning or more complex branching rules.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a row of light switches, one per letter position (digits have no switch, they are fixed). Trying every possible combination of switch positions (on/off, meaning uppercase/lowercase) produces every valid output string. This is a direct decision tree: each switch doubles the number of possible outcomes.

blocks.caption: Only letter positions have a switch to toggle; digit positions are fixed.

items: Walk the string one character at a time.
If the character is a letter, try both lowercase and uppercase, recursing after each choice.
If the character is a digit, there is only one choice, so simply continue to the next position.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
s = "a1b2". Position 0 ('a') is a letter, position 1 ('1') is a digit, position 2 ('b') is a letter, position 3 ('2') is a digit.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Since there are 2 letters, each with 2 case choices, there are 2*2 = 4 total outputs: ["a1b2", "a1B2", "A1b2", "A1B2"], matching a valid expected output set for this input.
5. How Should We Think?

An iterative approach builds up the full result set level by level: starting with just the empty string, each character either doubles every existing partial result (for a letter, appending both cases) or extends each one unchanged (for a digit). This is correct and simple but keeps every intermediate partial result in memory as full string copies at every step.

A recursive backtracking approach instead builds ONE mutable character array, trying each choice at each position by directly modifying that single array before recursing, and reports a complete string only when every position has been decided, avoiding repeated string copying at every level.
6. Brute Force Solution
Iteratively build the full result set, doubling it at every letter position (extending with both cases) and simply extending unchanged at every digit position.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n * 2^L)","n is the string length, L the number of letters, 2^L total outputs each built character by character"],["Space","O(n * 2^L)","Every intermediate result list, growing at each letter position"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: This is asymptotically similar to the backtracking version; the main difference is intermediate memory usage from rebuilding full string copies at every level rather than mutating one shared buffer.
8. Optimize the Solution

Use a single mutable character array shared across the recursion. At each position, if it is a letter, set it to lowercase and recurse, then set it to uppercase and recurse; if it is a digit, just recurse unchanged. When the array is fully decided (index reaches the string length), record a copy of it as one complete output.

items: Convert the string to a mutable character array once.
Recurse position by position: branch on letters, pass through digits.
At the base case (end of the array), record the current array contents as one output string.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Generating all combinations of independent binary choices is the simplest form of the backtracking template: branch, recurse, and (implicitly, since arrays are mutable) undo by simply overwriting on the next branch.
Positions with only one possible value (digits here) need no branching at all, simply passing through the recursion.
Using one shared mutable buffer instead of rebuilding full string copies at every level keeps extra space proportional to the string length, not the output size.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Letter Case Permutation is solved with straightforward backtracking over a shared mutable character array: letters branch into lowercase and uppercase choices, digits pass through unchanged, and a complete string is recorded once every position has been decided, generating all 2^L possible case combinations.
